args.text:
The microwaves are made inside the oven by an electron tube called a magnetron. They bounce around the metal inside of the oven, and that's where the tucker soaks them up. Microwaves make the water molecules in food jiggle about, and that makes the heat that cooks it. That's why food with a lot of water in it, like fresh veggies, cooks quicker than other tucker. The microwave energy turns into heat as the food soaks it up, and it doesn't make your food "radioactive" or "contaminated."

Now, the heat's made right there in the food, but microwave ovens don't cook food from the "inside out." When you cook something thick, the outer layers get heated and cooked mostly by the microwaves, while the inside cooks mainly by heat conducted in from those hot outer layers.

Microwave cooking can use less energy than ordinary cooking, cos the food cooks faster and the energy only heats the food, not the whole oven compartment. Cooking in the microwave doesn't knock the goodness out of your tucker any more than ordinary cooking does. Fact is, food done in a microwave oven may hang onto more of its vitamins and minerals, cos microwave ovens can cook quicker and without adding water.

You use glass, paper, ceramic or plastic containers in the microwave cos microwaves go straight through those materials. The microwaves can't heat containers like that, but they can still get hot from the heat of the food cooking inside them. Some plastic containers shouldn't go in a microwave oven at all, cos the heat of the food inside can melt them. As a rule, metal pans or alfoil shouldn't go in a microwave oven either, as the microwaves bounce off them, so the food cooks unevenly and the oven could cop some damage. The instructions that come with each microwave oven tell you which kinds of containers to use. They also cover how to test a container to see whether it can go in a microwave oven or not.

Steering Clear of Burns from Super-Heated Water in Microwave Ovens

The FDA has had reports of serious skin burns or scalds to people's hands and faces from hot water bursting out of a cup after it'd been overheated in a microwave oven. Super-heated water (water heated past its boiling temperature) doesn't look like it's boiling, and it happens when water is heated on its own in a clean cup. If water's been super-heated, the slightest bump or movement, like picking up the cup or tipping in a spoonful of instant coffee, can set off a violent eruption, with the boiling water exploding out of the cup. Putting something like instant coffee or sugar in before you heat it cuts that risk right down.

Follow the precautions and recommendations in your microwave oven's instruction manual to the letter, especially on heating times. When you're working out the best time settings to heat water to the temperature you want, make sure you don't go over the recommended heating times.
